This frozen takeaway page from Faros (an excerpt of the "AI Engineering Impact Report 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash") reports that the incidents-to-PR ratio rose 242.7% as teams moved from low to high AI adoption, and that monthly incidents rose 57.9%. The page's headline says the probability of a production incident per merged code change "has more than tripled." That claim is not supported as stated: the page itself says the figure is a ratio, not a probability. The comparison is also observational, so it does not show that AI caused the change. The full report was not captured, so this brief covers only the takeaway excerpt.

## Key Signals
- **Measured (page excerpt):** The incidents-to-PR ratio is up 242.7% as teams move from low to high AI adoption. The comparison is within each organization, between its periods of lowest and highest AI adoption.
  - *Qualification:* The page says this is a ratio, not a probability. A single PR can be linked to multiple incidents, and not every incident traces directly to the most recent merge.
- **Unsupported headline:** "For every code change merged, the probability of a production incident has more than tripled."
  - *Mismatch:* The body measures an incidents-to-PR ratio, not a per-change probability. The page explicitly disclaims the probability reading, so the headline should not be treated as an established finding. (Arithmetic note, my interpretation: +242.7% is about 3.4x, which is consistent with "more than tripled" only as a ratio, not a probability.)
- **Measured (page excerpt):** Monthly incidents are up 57.9%.
  - *Qualification:* The page excerpt does not give the baseline, the unit of aggregation (per org, per team, or total), or how this relates to the low-to-high adoption comparison. Whether it uses the same periods is unstated.
- **Population (page excerpt):** The report draws on two years of telemetry from 22,000 developers and more than 4,000 teams on the Faros platform.
  - *Qualification:* Selection into the Faros platform and how adoption levels were defined are not described in the excerpt.
- **Causality (authored context, not source claim):** The period comparison is observational. It is not a randomized causal effect and does not show that AI caused the change. The captured page reports no randomized effect.
- **Capture gap (collector note):** The full report was not captured.

## Technical Details
- Metric: incidents-to-PR ratio, i.e., incidents relative to merged pull requests. The page's caveats say PR-to-incident linkage is imperfect (one PR can link to multiple incidents, and an incident may not trace to the latest merge).
- Design: within-organization comparison of metric change between periods of lowest and highest AI adoption. The page describes this as measuring what AI is producing across the full software development lifecycle.
- Data: two years of telemetry, 22,000 developers, more than 4,000 teams, on the Faros platform.
- Not provided in the excerpt: how AI adoption was measured, how incidents were linked to PRs, the absolute rates, confidence intervals or uncertainty, controls for time or other confounders, and the length of the periods compared.

## Business Relevance
- The data suggests that incident load per merged PR rose in periods of higher AI adoption within these organizations (ratio +242.7%). It does not establish that AI caused this, and it does not show a tripled probability of incident per change.
- In customer or leadership conversations, the figure should be described as a ratio from an observational comparison. Quoting the headline as "probability tripled" would contradict the page's own qualification.
- Monthly incidents up 57.9% is a separate measure with no baseline in the excerpt, so it should not be combined with the ratio figure.
- The source is a vendor (Faros) reporting on its own platform data, which matters when weighing it. The excerpt does not discuss independent validation.

## Open Questions
- How was "low" versus "high" AI adoption defined and measured, and how long were the periods?
- Did time trends, team growth, changes in incident reporting, or PR size and volume shift between periods, and were they controlled for?
- Did PR counts rise, did incident counts rise, or both? The ratio alone does not say which drove the change.
- What are the absolute baselines, and what are the variation and uncertainty around 242.7% and 57.9%?
- What is the baseline and scope of the 57.9% monthly incidents figure?
- How representative are Faros customers of the wider industry?
- What does the full report say about causality and the other lifecycle metrics?

- Read the full "AI Engineering Impact Report 2026: The Acceleration Whiplash" for methodology, definitions and uncertainty.
- Look for other Faros pages covering how AI adoption and incident-to-PR linkage are measured.

## Summary
The page excerpt reports a randomized trial in which the probability of an incident within 7 days was 0.12 in the treated arm and 0.04 in the control arm, among randomized participants. The excerpt gives no sample sizes, uncertainty intervals, intervention definition or incident definition, so the size and reliability of the difference can't be judged from this page. A note labeled "gap; authored context" says the trial does not report an incidents-to-PR ratio. That note is supplied context, not a measurement from the trial.

## Key Signals
- **Measured (frozen page excerpt):** Incident probability within 7 days was 0.12 (treated) vs 0.04 (control), among randomized participants.
  - The absolute difference is 0.08 (8 percentage points), and the treated-arm probability is 3 times the control-arm probability. These are my arithmetic on the two reported figures, not statements from the page.
  - The direction is higher incidents in the treated arm. The excerpt does not say whether this was expected.
  - No confidence interval, p-value, sample size or event count is supplied. Whether the difference is statistically reliable is unknown.
- **Design:** The excerpt describes the study as randomized, which would normally support a causal reading of an arm difference. The excerpt gives no detail on how randomization, blinding, follow-up completeness or analysis were handled, so the strength of any causal conclusion can't be verified here.
- **Authored context (not the trial's own statement):** The note says the trial does not report an incidents-to-PR ratio. The page therefore offers no per-PR denominator, and incident probability per randomized participant shouldn't be converted into or compared with a per-PR rate.
- **Not supported by the page:** No claim that the treatment is beneficial, or that it is safe or unsafe in general. Only the two probabilities are given.

## Technical Details
- **Metric:** Probability of an incident within a 7-day window. The denominator is randomized participants, per arm.
- **Arms:** Treated and control. The excerpt doesn't say what the treatment is, what an "incident" is, or what a "participant" is (person, team, repository, etc.).
- **Missing:** Arm sizes, number of incidents, allocation ratio, handling of dropouts, analysis method (e.g., intention-to-treat), and uncertainty.
- **Other:** The page metadata gives no publication date or authors, and the title and URL use "synthetic". The excerpt doesn't say whether the data are real or simulated.

## Business Relevance
- If the figures are valid, the treated arm had a higher 7-day incident probability (0.12 vs 0.04 among randomized participants). That would be a caution for anyone considering the treatment. The lack of uncertainty estimates and intervention details limits how far this can inform decisions.
- Because no incidents-to-PR ratio is reported (per the authored note), the figures don't support claims about incident rates per code change or per PR.
- The page can't support general claims about the treatment's effect outside the trial's population and 7-day window.

## Open Questions
- What was the treatment, and what counts as an incident?
- What were the sample sizes and event counts per arm, and what are the confidence intervals or p-values?
- Was randomization at the participant level, and how were dropouts and missing follow-up handled?
- Is the data real or simulated, given the "synthetic" naming?
- Were other outcomes or longer follow-up measured? The excerpt only covers 7 days.
- Does the full trial really omit an incidents-to-PR ratio? That comes only from the authored note, which I can't verify.

## Useful Follow-ups
- Look for the full trial report or protocol, to check arm sizes, the incident definition, the analysis plan and uncertainty estimates.
- Look for any published method for the "synthetic" trial setup, to establish whether the data are simulated.
- If PR-level comparisons matter, find out whether per-PR data were collected, without assuming they exist.
